{{Short description|Subset that is closed and has no isolated points}}
In [[general topology]], a subset of a [[topological space]] is '''perfect''' if it is [[closed set|closed]] and has no [[isolated point]]s. Equivalently: the set <math>S</math> is perfect if  <math>S=S'</math>, where <math>S'</math> denotes the set of all [[Limit point|limit points]] of <math>S</math>, also known as the [[Derived set (mathematics)|derived set]] of <math>S</math>. (Some authors do not consider the empty set to be perfect.<ref>{{cite book|last=Jech|first=Thomas|authorlink = Thomas Jech|title=Set Theory (The Third Millenium Edition, revised and expanded)|series=Springer Monographs in Mathematics |date=2003|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-3-540-44085-7|page=40|doi=10.1007/3-540-44761-X}}</ref>)

In a perfect set, every point can be approximated arbitrarily well by other points from the set: given any point of <math>S</math> and any [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighborhood]] of the point, there is another point of <math>S</math> that lies within the neighborhood. Furthermore, any point of the space that can be so approximated by points of <math>S</math> belongs to <math>S</math>.

The term ''perfect space'' is also used, incompatibly, to refer to other properties of a topological space, such as being a [[G-delta space|G<sub>&delta;</sub> space]]. As another possible source of confusion, having the [[perfect set property]] is not the same as being a perfect set.

==Examples==

Examples of perfect subsets of the [[real line]] <math>\mathbb{R}</math> are the [[empty set]], all [[Closed interval|closed intervals]], the real line itself, and the [[Cantor set]]. The latter is noteworthy in that it is [[totally disconnected]].

Whether a set is perfect or not (and whether it is closed or not) depends on the surrounding space. For instance, the set <math>S=[0,1]\cap \Q</math> is perfect as a subset of the space <math>\Q</math> but not perfect as a subset of the space <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, since it fails to be [[closed set|closed]] in the latter.

== Connection with other topological properties ==

Every topological space can be written in a unique way as the disjoint union of a perfect set and a [[scattered space|scattered set]].<ref>Engelking, problem 1.7.10, p. 59</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3856152 |title = Uniqueness of decomposition into perfect set and scattered set - Mathematics Stack Exchange}}</ref>

[[Georg Cantor|Cantor]] proved that every closed subset of the real line can be uniquely written as the disjoint union of a perfect set and a [[countable set]].  This is also true more generally for all closed subsets of [[Polish space|Polish spaces]], in which case the theorem is known as the [[Cantor–Bendixson theorem]].

Cantor also showed that every non-empty perfect subset of the real line has [[cardinality]] <math>2^{\aleph_0}</math>, the [[cardinality of the continuum]]. These results are extended in  [[descriptive set theory]] as follows:
* If ''X'' is a [[complete metric space]] with no isolated points, then the [[Cantor space]] 2<sup>&omega;</sup> can be [[continuous function|continuously]] embedded into ''X''. Thus, ''X'' has cardinality at least <math>2^{\aleph_0}</math>. If ''X'' is a [[Separable space|separable]], complete metric space with no isolated points, the cardinality of ''X'' is exactly <math>2^{\aleph_0}</math>.  
* If ''X'' is a [[locally compact]] [[Hausdorff space]] with no isolated points, there is an [[injective function]] (not necessarily continuous) from the Cantor space to ''X'', and so ''X'' has cardinality at least <math>2^{\aleph_0}</math>.
